name: Freya Nakamura

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: I am with the Work Futures Panel. We are independent, with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, political parties or government; we sell nothing and campaign for no side. What you tell me stays confidential. What happens on an ordinary shift at the internet service centre?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I take calls from people whose connection drops in the middle of work or a family film. I check the outage map, ask about the lights on the router, and book an engineer if the line needs one. I sometimes use an AI draft for the call note, but I check the street and account number myself; the angry part of the call is still mine.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: And what is happening at home while those shifts carry on?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: Dev, my partner, delivers plants for a nursery and brings home a regular wage, but it wouldn't meet our whole mortgage. Our son lives elsewhere and pays his own bills. We have about five months of expenses saved; I like that space, but I don't want to spend it proving that a hobby is a job.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AI Plateau. "Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway."

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell my work friend the draft notes are useful when they get the street right. The person with no connection still wants me to explain what an engineer can do today. I don't see the service line disappearing in this picture.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I think our shifts continue and Dev keeps his delivery rounds. Five months saved lets us handle a repair without turning every meal into a calculation. I still check the automated note because a false outage can waste my next call.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: In 2026 I'll keep taking the fault calls and checking the AI draft against the outage map before sending it. If the plateau carries on in its first year, I'll keep that same routine and our ordinary household budget. I won't buy another service subscription just to chase a quicker answer.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm enough. A nuisance on a screen doesn't threaten the mortgage in this picture. I like the part where I can still tell a customer when a technician is actually coming.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What does a mistaken outage note cost you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A wrong outage notice sends three streets calling back before lunch. Then I have to correct the notes and apologise to each person. That is why I keep the map open beside the draft.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you use the extra time for anything?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I might finish the shift on time and cook with Dev. That would be lovely, but I wouldn't call it a new income. A spare half-hour isn't a wage.

say: I'd keep **checking outage notes** before they reach customers.
I'd say the **service line** still needs someone to explain an engineer visit.
think: I expect our **paid shifts** and Dev's deliveries to continue.
I treat five months saved as **repair money**, not permission to buy needless tools.
do: Keep taking **connection-fault calls** and check existing AI drafts against the outage map.
Keep our **ordinary household budget** while pay and prices carry on.
feel: **Calm** about wages and mortgage, with irritation at avoidable bad notes.
S0.quote: A wrong outage notice sends three streets calling back before lunch.
fieldNote: Her occasional **AI drafting** already exists; checking the outage map is normal work, not new AI learning.
Five months of expenses and Dev's **regular delivery wage** make this mild picture manageable.
She values an **accurate visit time** more than a faster but false note.

steps.text: Keep taking paid connection-fault calls and check AI notes against outage map

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Steady Disruption. "Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust."

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say the easy password calls will go to the machine first. A person still needs to sort out a bad engineer booking or a whole street wrongly marked as connected. I'd want the new fault-map tool tested against actual outages before it starts writing replies.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Fewer simple calls could mean fewer paid hours for the team. I can learn a new screen if it shows its sources, but I won't pretend my current habit of checking drafts is enough. I'd worry about a target that counts quick replies rather than fixed connections.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: This year I'll ask my supervisor for a paid practice shift on the new AI fault-map assistant and learn how to compare its suggested outage area with the live line readings. I'll log its wrong-street suggestions in our shared error book. I'll keep taking the complicated fault calls while those shifts remain paid as the change spreads.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, but I can see a piece of work I can do. I need the paid hours to learn it, not a lunchtime demonstration that ends before a customer calls. A smaller rota would still hurt us.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you write in the error book?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The street, the time, what the live line readings showed and whether a customer got the wrong message. A fault map that guesses the wrong street can waste a whole paid shift. I would show the book to the supervisor before the tool is made routine.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would tell you the new tool was worth using?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A week with fewer repeat calls and no false engineer bookings. I would also ask how many paid shifts the team keeps, because a clever tool can work well for customers and still cost us hours. Both things can be true.

say: I'd say **password calls** may disappear before difficult faults do.
I'd ask for **paid practice** and a record of wrong-street fault-map suggestions.
think: I fear **paid hours** could shrink even if complex faults remain.
I can learn **new fault-map checks**, beyond my occasional use of draft notes.
do: Learn the **new AI fault-map assistant** on a paid practice shift by checking suggested areas against live line readings.
Log **wrong-street suggestions** in the shared error book while continuing paid complex fault calls.
feel: **Anxious** about fewer paid hours, with some control through practical checking.
S1.quote: A fault map that guesses the wrong street can waste a whole paid shift.
fieldNote: She commits to **new AI learning**: testing suggested outage areas against live line readings on paid time.
The **error book** captures wrong-street messages before the tool becomes routine.
She expects **fewer simple calls** could cut paid hours despite remaining complex cases.

steps.text: Learn new AI fault-map assistant on paid shift by comparing suggestions with live readings
Log wrong-street errors and keep taking complex fault calls while paid

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2028. "Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare."

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell Dev that full thinking AI in 2028 could settle most line faults without our contact-centre queue. The hands-on router visit might last until robots around 2031, but I wouldn't promise a lifetime from it. I'd ask management for the paid-hour plan in writing.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I expect the phone rota could be cut heavily, maybe my whole week. Dev's nursery wage won't carry the mortgage alone, and five months saved isn't an income. I've fitted routers for neighbours, but friendly thanks haven't paid a bill.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Now in 2026 I'll put a small notice in the neighbourhood board offering booked Saturday router setups for a stated fee, using my own tools and no customer list from work. I'll record the fee, parts and journey on each paid visit. If the contact-centre shifts disappear in the first year after 2028, I'll keep only visits that actually pay after travel and use the reserve according to our checked mortgage budget; I won't call the visits a full replacement wage.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Alarmed. A side job can be a useful thread, but the mortgage is a rope. I can test whether anybody pays before I lean on it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would make a router visit worth your Saturday?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A booking with a clear fee, the parts paid for and enough left after the bus to make the time worthwhile. I can fit a router in a kitchen, but home visits will not cover our mortgage just because the call queue closes. I'd show Dev the receipts before counting them.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you give up first if the rota disappeared?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The planned new patio chairs can wait. I'd keep the travel money for actual paid visits and the reserve for mortgage bills. Our son has his own rent, so I won't put his money on the page.

say: I'd warn Dev **2028 AGI** could remove contact-centre calls before 2031 hands-on robots.
I'd ask management for a **written paid-hour plan**.
think: I expect a **large rota cut**, perhaps my entire week.
I know Dev's wage and **five months saved** cannot carry the mortgage alone for long.
do: Advertise **booked paid router setups** on the neighbourhood board in 2026, using personal tools and no employer customer list.
Record **fees, parts and travel**; if 2028 call shifts disappear, keep only visits paying after travel.
Delay **patio chairs** and budget the reserve against mortgage bills if paid calls end.
feel: **Alarmed** by likely lost shifts and an unproven side income.
S2.quote: I can fit a router in a kitchen, but home visits will not cover our mortgage just because the call queue closes.
fieldNote: She tests **paid physical setups** before treating weekend visits as household income.
The first-year plan keeps only **net-paying visits** after travel and uses a checked mortgage budget.
She protects privacy by avoiding the **employer customer list** and does not count her grown son's money.

steps.text: Advertise booked paid Saturday router setups using personal tools and no employer customer list
Record visit fees parts and travel; keep only net-paying visits if 2028 call shifts disappear
Delay patio chairs and budget five-month reserve for mortgage if calls end

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2031. "Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast."

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years lets us see whether people pay for physical setup help before the 2031 AI reaches the centre. Robots might do more of that work around 2034. I would not tell anyone that a router in a kitchen is a permanent safe job.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I could build a small round of booked visits while keeping my contact-centre pay. More customers may learn to ask AI what to do, so the service must be something I physically fix and people really buy. I won't empty five months of savings to buy a van or promise Dev that the round will grow.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: This year I'll keep a ledger of paid Saturday setups, parts and travel and ask each customer for permission to use a short review on the noticeboard. I'll keep my centre shifts while they pay and put net visit receipts into a separate repair reserve. In the first year after 2031, if calls are cut, I'll continue the booked visits only while net receipts justify them and the work remains safe for me to do.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, but not rushed into buying anything. Five years lets me see repeat customers, not just neighbours being kind. The 2034 robot date still makes a big loan foolish.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would count as a real customer, not a favour?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A stranger who books a time, pays the stated fee and calls back for another job. Three paid visits are evidence; three neighbours saying thanks are not. I would keep their addresses out of any public review.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you make the weekend round bigger?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Only if I can still rest and Dev and I can see net receipts after parts and travel for several months. I would not turn every Saturday into work because an AI date appeared on a card. A small round that pays is better than a full diary of favours.

say: I'd test **paid setup demand** over years rather than assume a safe new career.
I'd tell friends **2034 robots** may reach physical setup after 2031 AGI reaches calls.
think: I can build **booked visits** while current call pay continues.
I doubt a bigger round warrants a **van loan** or spending our five-month reserve.
do: Log **paid visit receipts**, parts and travel and request permission for customer reviews without public addresses.
Keep **paid centre shifts** and place net visit receipts in a separate repair reserve.
Continue **booked safe visits** after 2031 call cuts only while receipts exceed parts and travel.
feel: **Anxious** about future calls, with time to measure genuine paying demand.
S3.quote: Three paid visits are evidence; three neighbours saying thanks are not.
fieldNote: The **five-year window** turns weekend visits into a measured trial, using receipts rather than favours.
She keeps **current paid shifts** and saves net visit money rather than buying a van.
Physical work is only a **conditional bridge** because robots may reach it around 2034.

steps.text: Log paid setup receipts parts and travel; use customer reviews only with permission
Continue safe paid setups after 2031 call cuts only if receipts exceed parts and travel
Put net visit receipts into separate repair reserve without buying a van

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2036. "Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans."

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say a decade lets people check what work pays and what their bodies can keep doing. By 2036 I'd be sixty-eight, and hands-on robots come around 2039 in this picture. I cannot tell our son that I will have stopped working by then.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would like Sundays free by that age, perhaps all the weekends. But five months saved today is not a retirement income, and Dev's delivery wage may change too. I would trust a page of actual household figures more than a neat date.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Starting in 2026, Dev and I will review the mortgage balance, savings and real net visit receipts each year. I'll keep paid centre work while it exists and keep weekend visits small enough to protect a rest day. If AGI ends calls in the first year after 2036, I'll stop any visits I can no longer do safely. If the work is safe, I'll reduce visits only when checked household income covers the mortgage and essentials; otherwise I'll take paid bookings I can manage.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious about whether my hands and our money will agree at sixty-eight. The long warning is helpful because I can measure both. It doesn't give me a pension figure or a free house.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would tell you to stop weekend visits?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The yearly figures showing mortgage and essentials covered without those fees, or my hands telling me the work is unsafe. At sixty-eight I want a choice about Sunday visits, not a date somebody invented for me. I would check both before cancelling a booking.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell your grown son?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell him we are checking our own income and savings. He has his own bills, and I won't ask him to promise support for a future I can't price. He can know the plan without becoming the plan.

say: I'd say **ten years** permits checks on real earnings and physical ability.
I'd explain **2036 AGI** still threatens centre calls if I need the wage then.
think: I want fewer **weekend visits** by sixty-eight if the money permits.
I cannot assume five months saved or Dev's wage becomes **retirement income**.
do: Review **mortgage and receipts**, plus savings, with Dev every year from 2026.
Keep **paid centre shifts** and a rest day while weekend visits remain safe.
After 2036 call loss, stop **unsafe visits**; otherwise take paid bookings until checked income covers mortgage and essentials.
feel: **Anxious** about future income and physical ability, with time to measure both.
S4.quote: At sixty-eight I want a choice about Sunday visits, not a date somebody invented for me.
fieldNote: She makes no claim to a **pension** or dependable support from her adult son.
Her annual **mortgage and receipts check** determines whether she can reduce visits after 2036.
A **rest day** and safe hands remain limits even if extra paid visits are available.

steps.text: Defer reducing safe visits until checked income covers mortgage and essentials
Keep paid centre shifts and a rest day while weekend visits stay safe
Stop unsafe visits after 2036 call loss; otherwise book paid visits if income falls short

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028 worries me most because I couldn't turn a few router visits into a mortgage payment in two years. Written paid-hour dates from the centre and a clear picture of our bills would help. A receipt is a better promise than a forecast about my working life.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Whether people can still reach a person when the line is down. My neighbour once had to walk to our door because the online help needed an internet connection. I hope somebody asks customers that before closing a phone line.

headlineQuote: A receipt is a better promise than a forecast about my working life.
portrait: At **fifty-eight**, Freya explains internet faults, verifies AI-drafted notes and books engineer visits at a contact centre.
She has **secondary schooling**, typical pay, five months saved and a partner whose plant-delivery wage cannot meet the mortgage alone.
She learns a **new fault-map assistant** in Steady Disruption by testing its suggestions against live line readings.
Fast AGI prompts **paid router setup visits**; slower futures let her measure receipts before changing the amount of work she does.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028** could erase paid phone shifts before router setup visits can reliably meet the mortgage.
whatWouldHelp: **Written paid-hour dates** and a clear household bill picture would help her judge the gap.
